title: Optimising multipartite entanglement manipulation in quantum networks
authors: Shashank Shekhar, David Elkouss, Siddhartha Santra
abstract: Long-range, genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) between distant parties in a quantum network is a crucial resource for distributed quantum information processing. Through controlled manipulation of short-range GME states in the network via stochastic local operations aided by classical communication (SLOCC), long-range GME can be established between selected target nodes on demand. Optimizing such multipartite entanglement distribution protocols under constraints imposed by the network architecture, target-node set, and available resource budget is a key challenge in resource-efficient manipulation of GME. We present a general operational framework for manipulating GME in quantum networks by classifying the relevant networking operations into three broad primitives-inflation, deflation, and purification-reflecting their effect on the proliferation of GME through general bounds and illustrative examples. We show how these primitives can be combined to construct a broad class of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, enabling their systematic optimization, and demonstrate the framework with a simple example. Applying our approach to networks of Dür-Cirac-Tarrach states reveals a rich landscape of achievable end-to-end GME and accessible entanglement classes. More generally, our framework provides a systematic approach to the construction and optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols for scalable and resource-efficient GME distribution in quantum networks.
summary: This work presents a general operational framework to systematically optimize the distribution of multipartite entanglement in quantum networks. By classifying networking operations into inflation, deflation, and purification primitives, the authors provide systematic bounds and protocols for quantum repeaters. This advances the field by offering a comprehensive tool for resource-efficient GME distribution.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of optimizing the distribution of long-range Genuine Multipartite Entanglement (GME) on demand within quantum networks.
main_result: A general operational framework based on three primitives (inflation, deflation, purification) allows for the systematic optimization of multipartite quantum repeater protocols, showing that postselection can enhance entanglement beyond initial resource bounds.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework by classifying networking operations into inflation, deflation, and purification primitives, and applying this to analyze specific quantum repeater protocols.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a quantum network represented by a hypergraph, utilizing multipartite entangled states, specifically Dür-Cirac-Tarrach (DCT) states, as resources.
key_observables: Genuine Multipartite Concurrence (GMC), Localizable Multipartite Entanglement (LE), and fidelity.
important_parameters: Network architecture, target-node set, and resource budget.
main_assumptions: Local operations are restricted to Stochastic Local Operations and Classical Communication (SLOCC).
figures_summary: Figures schematically represent the hypergraph network structure and compare the average output GMC of two different quantum repeater protocols (E1-M-QR vs. E2-M-QR) under various conditions, including postselection.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the operational framework by defining the three primitives (inflation, deflation, purification), derives bounds for GMC under these operations, and then applies this framework to compare and optimize specific multipartite quantum repeater protocols using DCT states.
why_interesting: The systematic classification of entanglement manipulation primitives (inflation, deflation, purification) provides a powerful, general tool for analyzing resource constraints in quantum network design, which is highly relevant to quantum information theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic representation of a multipartite quantum network modeled as a hypergraph. (a) The network is composed of elementary three-qubit entangled units, with each blue triangular unit representing a hyperedge and the orange nodes representing qubits. (b) Enlarged view of the highlighted region in (a), illustrating how elementary hyperedges are connected through shared nodes to form a larger multipartite network.

FIG. 2. Multipartite entanglement class of the final DCT state as a function of PCM iterations (i) of the M-QR protocol for different initial parameters of tripartite DCT states. (a) PCM protocol. (b) PCM protocol with end-to-end purification. The regions correspond to different entanglement classes: red (S1) GHZ-class states identified by a nonzero three-tangle; blue (S2) genuinely multipartite entangled states that may belong to either the GHZ or W class; green (S3) biseparable states; light green (S4) fully separable states.

FIG. 4. Success probability psucc of the two triangular M-QR protocols as a function of SQDN strength p. E2 M-QR retains psucc = 1 up to p ≈0.087 before dropping sharply to zero, whereas E1 M-QR declines gradually and remains nonzero up to p ≈0.125. The curves cross near p ≈0.087, above which E1 M-QR has both higher Cg and psucc.

FIG. 3. Average (⟨Cg⟩, solid) and best postselected (Cgps, dashed) genuine multipartite concurrence versus SQDN strength p, comparing the all-BSM protocol E1 M−QR (blue) and the hybrid BSM+Hadamard protocol E2 M−QR (red). E1 M−QR dominates both metrics over the full range of p.

FIG. 5. Difference in genuine multipartite concurrence of average state, ∆= Cg(¯ρ)E1 −Cg(¯ρ)E2, between the E2 M−QR and the E1 M−QR under ASAP scheduling with probabilistic link generation, as a function of the per-attempt link success probability pg and the memory depolarizing rate (denoted p). Blue regions (∆< 0) indicate E2 M−QR performs better; red regions (∆> 0) indicate E1 M−QR performs better.
